Sherry Kutter, a University of Minnesota Extension Master Naturalist, first spotted the vine along the <a href="/430/Lake-Wobegon-Trail">Lake Wobegon Trail<\/a> in Holdingford. Officials have identified it as rough potato (Metaplexis japonica), a type of vining milkweed.<\/p><p>Rough potato is native to eastern Asia. It has not been previously reported in North America except in 1958 in cornfields near the Iowa State University campus in Ames where it may have been part of a research project during World War II. How rough potato arrived in Holdingford is a mystery.<\/p><p>Bob Dunning, Stearns County Agricultural Inspector, mapped the vines locations and notified landowners. The densest infestations are along the South Two River near a ballfield. Bob said &ldquo;I was surprised by the number of locations I found it in once I began scouting for it. I&rsquo;m grateful to Sherry for discovering this issue before it had become even more widespread. Rough Potato is a very aggressive climber and it has an amazing ability to completely cover other vegetation.&rdquo;<\/p><p>Because of the magnitude of the infestations, the <a href="/238/Parks">Stearns County Parks Department<\/a>, Conservation Corps Minnesota (CCM), and the Minnesota Department of Agriculture (MDA) began removing thousands of seedpods, each containing many seeds. This was done to prevent the infestation from spreading. Based upon experience with related vining milkweeds, a combination of herbicide treatment and manual removal over several years will bring down the infestations.<\/p><p>&ldquo;While we may never know how rough potato got to Stearns County, we can be diligent so this and other invasive plants don&rsquo;t spread throughout Minnesota,&rdquo; said Monika Chandler, MDA Invasive Species Specialist. &ldquo;Seeds and plant parts like to hitch a ride, so cleaning equipment, pets, and our clothes before leaving an area can help prevent the spread of unwanted plants.&rdquo;<\/p><p>There are no vining milkweeds native to Minnesota. Both black and pale swallow-worts are vining milkweeds and have been found at a limited number of locations in the state. Click on the link titled 10/14/2020 Sauk River Comprehensive Watershed Management Plan &ndash; Draft.<\/p><p>Please submit written comments (may be submitted electronically) by 4:30 pm on December 18th, 2020 to:<\/p><p>Sarah Boser<br>Water Resource Manager for the SRWD and Plan Coordinator for Sauk River 1W1P<br>642 Lincoln Road<br>Sauk Centre, MN 56378<br>320.352.2231<br><a href=\\"mailto:sarah@srwdmn.org\\">sarah@srwdmn.org<\/a><\/p><p>After completion of this review period, a summary of comments received will be provided to all who commented and the Sauk River Partnership will hold public hearing(s) (time and location to be determined according to COVID-19 restrictions in place at that time). To be notified of the public hearing time and location, please contact Sarah Boser using the previously noted contact information.<\/p><p>Thank you on behalf of the members of the Partnership.<\/p><ul><li>Douglas County<\/li><li>Douglas Soil and Water Conservation District<\/li><li>Pope County<\/li><li>Pope Soil and Water Conservation District<\/li><li>Sauk River Watershed District<\/li><li>Stearns County<\/li><li>Stearns Soil and Water Conservation District<\/li><li>Todd County<\/li><li>Todd Soil and Water Conservation District<\/li><\/ul><p>Many other agencies and community organizations participated in the creation of this local watershed management plan.      },\n        "title": {\n          "en": "MDH Doing COVID-19 Testing in St. Joseph this Week"\n        },\n        "description": {\n          "en": "<p>St. Joseph is one of several sites this week where MDH is offering no-barrier COVID-19 testing in response to increased community spread statewide. Testing is free and open to anyone from any community, with or without symptoms. <a href=\\"http://www.primarybio.com/r/stjoseph\\">Schedule an Appointment<\/a><\/p><p><strong>St. Joseph COVID-19 Community Testing Event<\/strong><br>Tuesday, Oct. 6 &ndash; Thursday, Oct. 8<br>12 to 6 p.m.<br>Clemens Field House, College of Saint Benedict<br><a href=\\"http://www.google.com/search?q=37+College+Ave+S+St.+Joseph,+MN+56374&rlz=1C1GCEA_enUS845US845&oq=37+College+Ave+S+St.+Joseph,+MN+56374&aqs=chrome..69i57j0l3.1124j0j7&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8#spf=1601920717380\\">37 College Ave S, St. Joseph<\/a><\/p><p>The Minnesota Department of Health is partnering with local public health officials and other community partners to offer access to the free, no-barrier COVID-19 testing the week of Oct. 5 in St. Joseph, Northfield, Willmar, Fairmont, Inver Grove Heights, Ely, and Cloquet.<\/p><p>As always with no-barrier testing opportunities, this testing will be free, available to anyone from any community who wants to be tested whether they have symptoms or not, and will not require insurance. The events are part of an effort to increase access to &ldquo;no-barrier&rdquo; COVID-19 testing following increased levels of community spread statewide. The Minnesota National Guard will continue providing logistical support for a number of these events.<\/p><p>&ldquo;We know some people who contract COVID-19 might not even know they have it,&rdquo; Minnesota Department of Health Commissioner Jan Malcolm said. &ldquo;That&rsquo;s part of what makes this virus so dangerous and makes easy access to testing and quick results so important. All who contract the virus are contagious and giving people a chance to get tested allows people to isolate if positive and let their close contacts know they should quarantine. Minnesotans in communities across the state understand the risk and are responding.&rdquo;<\/p><p>Health officials use testing data to identify communities that are experiencing workplace clusters, are close to bordering states, or haven&rsquo;t yet had larger-scale testing offered. This strategy will help increase the geographic balance of testing across Minnesota and respond where the health risk is greatest. Testing opportunities have been provided in Grand Rapids, Pine City, Waseca, Bloomington, Maplewood, Moorhead, Marshall, Thief River Falls and Bemidji.<\/p><p>Testing will be done with a nasal swab, processed either by Mayo Clinic Laboratories or the University of Minnesota, through the lab capacity created by the testing partnership.<\/p><p>Anyone who wants to be tested is encouraged to come, even if they don&rsquo;t have symptoms of COVID-19. No insurance or identification is needed. To avoid long lines, people are encouraged to pre-register for a time slot. Those who are unable to sign up online or need interpretation can call 1-855-612-0677 for assistance.<\/p><p><strong>What to bring<\/strong><\/p><ul><li>Wear a mask or face covering if you can.<\/li><li>Bring your sign-up confirmation text or email if you can.<\/li><li>You do not need to show identification or insurance information.<\/li><\/ul><p><strong>What to expect at the event<\/strong><\/p><ul><li>If you signed up for an appointment online or by phone, staff will ask to see your confirmation text or email, or you can tell them your name, birthdate, and address.<\/li><li>If you did not sign up for an appointment ahead of time, a greeter will register you when you get to the event. You will need to provide your name and contact information. This information is given to staff to contact you with your test results.<\/li><li>Please arrive at the site close to the time of your scheduled visit. Staff will check you in when you arrive and tell you where to go. Testing sites are designed to ensure social distancing and proper cleaning to keep you safe.<\/li><li>A health care worker will gently insert what looks like a long Q-tip into your nose and swirl it for a few seconds in order to get a good sample. It will then be removed and put in a vial to be sent to a lab for testing.<\/li><\/ul><p><strong>What to Expect: Getting a nasal swab at a testing event<\/strong><\/p><p>MDH uses the nasal swab method shown in this video at all their community testing events.<\/p><p><a href=\\"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DEiapWRTPIU&feature=emb_logo&ab_channel=mnhealth\\">https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DEiapWRTPIU&amp;feature=emb_logo&amp;ab_channel=mnhealth<\/a><\/p>"\n        },\n        "newsassets": {\n          "iv": []\n        }\n      },\n      "draft": {\n        "data": {\n          "Date": {\n            "iv": "2020-10-05T05:00:00Z"\n          },\n          "title": {\n            "en": "MDH Doing COVID-19 Testing in St. Joseph this Week"\n          },\n          "description": {\n            "en": "<p>St. Joseph is one of several sites this week where MDH is offering no-barrier COVID-19 testing in response to increased community spread statewide. Those who are unable to sign up online or need interpretation can call 1-855-612-0677 for assistance.<\/p><p><strong>What to bring<\/strong><\/p><ul><li>Wear a mask or face covering if you can.<\/li><li>Bring your sign-up confirmation text or email if you can.<\/li><li>You do not need to show identification or insurance information.<\/li><\/ul><p><strong>What to expect at the event<\/strong><\/p><ul><li>If you signed up for an appointment online or by phone, staff will ask to see your confirmation text or email, or you can tell them your name, birthdate, and address.<\/li><li>If you did not sign up for an appointment ahead of time, a greeter will register you when you get to the event. You will need to provide your name and contact information. This information is given to staff to contact you with your test results.<\/li><li>Please arrive at the site close to the time of your scheduled visit. Staff will check you in when you arrive and tell you where to go. Testing sites are designed to ensure social distancing and proper cleaning to keep you safe.<\/li><li>A health care worker will gently insert what looks like a long Q-tip into your nose and swirl it for a few seconds in order to get a good sample. It will then be removed and put in a vial to be sent to a lab for testing.<\/li><\/ul><p><strong>What to Expect: Getting a nasal swab at a testing event<\/strong><\/p><p>MDH uses the nasal swab method shown in this video at all their community testing events.<\/p><p><a href=\\"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DEiapWRTPIU&feature=emb_logo&ab_channel=mnhealth\\">https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DEiapWRTPIU&amp;feature=emb_logo&amp;ab_channel=mnhealth<\/a><\/p>"\n decades has been discovered in Stearns County. Sherry Kutter, a University of Minnesota Extension Master Naturalist, first spotted the vine along the <a href=\\"/430/Lake-Wobegon-Trail\\">Lake Wobegon Trail<\/a> in Holdingford. Officials have identified it as rough potato (Metaplexis japonica), a type of vining milkweed.<\/p><p>Rough potato is native to eastern Asia. It has not been previously reported in North America except in 1958 in cornfields near the Iowa State University campus in Ames where it may have been part of a research project during World War II. How rough potato arrived in Holdingford is a mystery.<\/p><p>Bob Dunning, Stearns County Agricultural Inspector, mapped the vines locations and notified landowners. The densest infestations are along the South Two River near a ballfield. Bob said &ldquo;I was surprised by the number of locations I found it in once I began scouting for it. I&rsquo;m grateful to Sherry for discovering this issue before it had become even more widespread. Rough Potato is a very aggressive climber and it has an amazing ability to completely cover other vegetation.&rdquo;<\/p><p>Because of the magnitude of the infestations, the <a href=\\"/238/Parks\\">Stearns County Parks Department<\/a>, Conservation Corps Minnesota (CCM), and the Minnesota Department of Agriculture (MDA) began removing thousands of seedpods, each containing many seeds. This was done to prevent the infestation from spreading. Based upon experience with related vining milkweeds, a combination of herbicide treatment and manual removal over several years will bring down the infestations.<\/p><p>&ldquo;While we may never know how rough potato got to Stearns County, we can be diligent so this and other invasive plants don&rsquo;t spread throughout Minnesota,&rdquo; said Monika Chandler, MDA Invasive Species Specialist. &ldquo;Seeds and plant parts like to hitch a ride, so cleaning equipment, pets, and our clothes before leaving an area can help prevent the spread of unwanted plants.&rdquo;<\/p><p>There are no vining milkweeds native to Minnesota. Both black and pale swallow-worts are vining milkweeds and have been found at a limited number of locations in the state. If you see a vining milkweed, which has a distinctive milkweed seedpod, in Stearns County report it to Bob Dunning at <a href=\\"mailto:robert.dunning@co.stearns.mn.us\\">Robert.dunning@co.stearns.mn.us<\/a> or 320-656-6578 or in other counties report it to the MDA&rsquo;s Arrest the Pest line at <a href=\\"mailto:arrest.the.pest@state.mn.us\\">arrest.the.pest@state.mn.us<\/a> or 1-888-545-6684.<\/p><p>Work done by CCM and the MDA was supported by the Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund as recommended by the Legislative-Citizens Commission on Minnesota Resources.<\/p>"\n        },\n        "newsassets": {\n          "iv": [\n            "adcc946f-0095-4050-9236-0479d4ac6818",\n            "2974b78c-3d3d-4931-87e0-ac19e2d46609",\n            "4c48eaf5-fdda-45d9-bee3-3b8e4cd40cef",\n            "c29e53d9-bb6b-42e8-868c-71e718f7f73a"\n          ]\n        }\n      },\n      "draft": {\n        "data": {\n          "Date": {\n            "iv": "2020-09-25T05:00:00Z"\n          },\n          "title": {\n            "en": "Invasive Vine Spotted in Stearns County"\n          },\n          "description": {\n            "en": "<p>An invasive vine not seen in the United States in six decades has been discovered in Stearns County. "Important Property Tax Notice: Homestead Applications Due"\n        },\n        "description": {\n          "en": "<p>Property owners in Stearns County who have purchased or moved into a new home within the past year and need a homestead classification have until December 15, 2020 to file the application. The property tax homestead classification affects the amount of taxes that a property owner will pay in 2021 and may also affect the taxpayer&rsquo;s eligibility for a property tax refund.&nbsp;<\/p><p>A homestead application should be submitted to the County Assessor by December 15th if the use of the property owned or occupied as a qualifying relative has changed on or before December 1, 2020. Once homestead is granted, annual applications are not necessary unless they are requested by the County Assessor. Law requires notification to the County Assessor within 30 days of the change in homestead status due to a sale, move, or for any reason that would no longer qualify the property for the homestead classification.<\/p><p>A qualifying relative for homestead purposes depends on the type of property. The events are part of an effort to increase access to &ldquo;no-barrier&rdquo; COVID-19 testing following increased levels of community spread statewide. The Minnesota National Guard will continue providing logistical support for a number of these events.<\/p><p>&ldquo;We know some people who contract COVID-19 might not even know they have it,&rdquo; Minnesota Department of Health Commissioner Jan Malcolm said. &ldquo;That&rsquo;s part of what makes this virus so dangerous and makes easy access to testing and quick results so important. Minnesotans in communities across the state understand the risk and are responding.&rdquo;<\/p><p>Health officials use testing data to identify communities that are experiencing workplace clusters, are close to bordering states, or haven&rsquo;t yet had larger-scale testing offered. This strategy will help increase the geographic balance of testing across Minnesota and respond where the health risk is greatest. Testing opportunities have been provided in Grand Rapids, Pine City, Waseca, Bloomington, Maplewood, Moorhead, Marshall, Thief River Falls and Bemidji.<\/p><p>Testing will be done with a nasal swab, processed either by Mayo Clinic Laboratories or the University of Minnesota, through the lab capacity created by the testing partnership.<\/p><p>Anyone who wants to be tested is encouraged to come, even if they don&rsquo;t have symptoms of COVID-19. No insurance or identification is needed. To avoid long lines, people are encouraged to pre-register for a time slot.      },\n        "title": {\n          "en": "Invasive Vine Spotted in Stearns County"\n        },\n        "description": {\n          "en": "<p>An invasive vine not seen in the United States in six decades has been discovered in Stearns County. Sherry Kutter, a University of Minnesota Extension Master Naturalist, first spotted the vine along the <a href=\\"/430/Lake-Wobegon-Trail\\">Lake Wobegon Trail<\/a> in Holdingford. Officials have identified it as rough potato (Metaplexis japonica), a type of vining milkweed.<\/p><p>Rough potato is native to eastern Asia. It has not been previously reported in North America except in 1958 in cornfields near the Iowa State University campus in Ames where it may have been part of a research project during World War II. How rough potato arrived in Holdingford is a mystery.<\/p><p>Bob Dunning, Stearns County Agricultural Inspector, mapped the vines locations and notified landowners. The densest infestations are along the South Two River near a ballfield. Bob said &ldquo;I was surprised by the number of locations I found it in once I began scouting for it. I&rsquo;m grateful to Sherry for discovering this issue before it had become even more widespread. Rough Potato is a very aggressive climber and it has an amazing ability to completely cover other vegetation.&rdquo;<\/p><p>Because of the magnitude of the infestations, the <a href=\\"/238/Parks\\">Stearns County Parks Department<\/a>, Conservation Corps Minnesota (CCM), and the Minnesota Department of Agriculture (MDA) began removing thousands of seedpods, each containing many seeds. This was done to prevent the infestation from spreading. Based upon experience with related vining milkweeds, a combination of herbicide treatment and manual removal over several years will bring down the infestations.<\/p><p>&ldquo;While we may never know how rough potato got to Stearns County, we can be diligent so this and other invasive plants don&rsquo;t spread throughout Minnesota,&rdquo; said Monika Chandler, MDA Invasive Species Specialist. &ldquo;Seeds and plant parts like to hitch a ride, so cleaning equipment, pets, and our clothes before leaving an area can help prevent the spread of unwanted plants.&rdquo;<\/p><p>There are no vining milkweeds native to Minnesota. Both black and pale swallow-worts are vining milkweeds and have been found at a limited number of locations in the state. If you see a vining milkweed, which has a distinctive milkweed seedpod, in Stearns County report it to Bob Dunning at <a href=\\"mailto:robert.dunning@co.stearns.mn.us\\">Robert.dunning@co.stearns.mn.us<\/a> or 320-656-6578 or in other counties report it to the MDA&rsquo;s Arrest the Pest line at <a href=\\"mailto:arrest.the.pest@state.mn.us\\">arrest.the.pest@state.mn.us<\/a> or 1-888-545-6684.<\/p><p>Work done by CCM and the MDA was supported by the Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund as recommended by the Legislative-Citizens Commission on Minnesota Resources.<\/p>"\n        },\n        "newsassets": {\n          "iv": [\n            "adcc946f-0095-4050-9236-0479d4ac6818",\n            "2974b78c-3d3d-4931-87e0-ac19e2d46609",\n            "4c48eaf5-fdda-45d9-bee3-3b8e4cd40cef",\n            "c29e53d9-bb6b-42e8-868c-71e718f7f73a"\n          ]\n        }\n      },\n      "draft": {\n        "data": {\n          "Date": {\n            "iv": "2020-09-25T05:00:00Z"\n          },\n          "title": {\n            "en": "Invasive Vine Spotted in Stearns County"\n          },\n          "description": {\n            "en": "<p>An invasive vine not seen in the United States in six decades has been discovered in Stearns County. "Important Property Tax Notice: Homestead Applications Due"\n        },\n        "description": {\n          "en": "<p>Property owners in Stearns County who have purchased or moved into a new home within the past year and need a homestead classification have until December 15, 2020 to file the application. The property tax homestead classification affects the amount of taxes that a property owner will pay in 2021 and may also affect the taxpayer&rsquo;s eligibility for a property tax refund.&nbsp;<\/p><p>A homestead application should be submitted to the County Assessor by December 15th if the use of the property owned or occupied as a qualifying relative has changed on or before December 1, 2020. Once homestead is granted, annual applications are not necessary unless they are requested by the County Assessor. Law requires notification to the County Assessor within 30 days of the change in homestead status due to a sale, move, or for any reason that would no longer qualify the property for the homestead classification.<\/p><p>A qualifying relative for homestead purposes depends on the type of property. For agricultural property, a qualifying relative includes a child, grandchild, sibling or parent of the owner or owner&rsquo;s spouse. For residential property it also includes the owner&rsquo;s uncle, aunt, nephew, or niece.&nbsp;<\/p><p><a href=\\"https://services.co.stearns.mn.us/homestead/\\">Apply for homestead classification<\/a>. The Minnesota National Guard will continue providing logistical support for a number of these events.<\/p><p>&ldquo;We know some people who contract COVID-19 might not even know they have it,&rdquo; Minnesota Department of Health Commissioner Jan Malcolm said. &ldquo;That&rsquo;s part of what makes this virus so dangerous and makes easy access to testing and quick results so important.      },\n        "title": {\n          "en": "Invasive Vine Spotted in Stearns County"\n        },\n        "description": {\n          "en": "<p>An invasive vine not seen in the United States in six decades has been discovered in Stearns County. Sherry Kutter, a University of Minnesota Extension Master Naturalist, first spotted the vine along the <a href=\\"/430/Lake-Wobegon-Trail\\">Lake Wobegon Trail<\/a> in Holdingford. Officials have identified it as rough potato (Metaplexis japonica), a type of vining milkweed.<\/p><p>Rough potato is native to eastern Asia. It has not been previously reported in North America except in 1958 in cornfields near the Iowa State University campus in Ames where it may have been part of a research project during World War II. How rough potato arrived in Holdingford is a mystery.<\/p><p>Bob Dunning, Stearns County Agricultural Inspector, mapped the vines locations and notified landowners. The densest infestations are along the South Two River near a ballfield. Bob said &ldquo;I was surprised by the number of locations I found it in once I began scouting for it. I&rsquo;m grateful to Sherry for discovering this issue before it had become even more widespread. Rough Potato is a very aggressive climber and it has an amazing ability to completely cover other vegetation.&rdquo;<\/p><p>Because of the magnitude of the infestations, the <a href=\\"/238/Parks\\">Stearns County Parks Department<\/a>, Conservation Corps Minnesota (CCM), and the Minnesota Department of Agriculture (MDA) began removing thousands of seedpods, each containing many seeds. This was done to prevent the infestation from spreading. Based upon experience with related vining milkweeds, a combination of herbicide treatment and manual removal over several years will bring down the infestations.<\/p><p>&ldquo;While we may never know how rough potato got to Stearns County, we can be diligent so this and other invasive plants don&rsquo;t spread throughout Minnesota,&rdquo; said Monika Chandler, MDA Invasive Species Specialist. &ldquo;Seeds and plant parts like to hitch a ride, so cleaning equipment, pets, and our clothes before leaving an area can help prevent the spread of unwanted plants.&rdquo;<\/p><p>There are no vining milkweeds native to Minnesota. Both black and pale swallow-worts are vining milkweeds and have been found at a limited number of locations in the state. If you see a vining milkweed, which has a distinctive milkweed seedpod, in Stearns County report it to Bob Dunning at <a href=\\"mailto:robert.dunning@co.stearns.mn.us\\">Robert.dunning@co.stearns.mn.us<\/a> or 320-656-6578 or in other counties report it to the MDA&rsquo;s Arrest the Pest line at <a href=\\"mailto:arrest.the.pest@state.mn.us\\">arrest.the.pest@state.mn.us<\/a> or 1-888-545-6684.<\/p><p>Work done by CCM and the MDA was supported by the Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund as recommended by the Legislative-Citizens Commission on Minnesota Resources.<\/p>"\n        },\n        "newsassets": {\n          "iv": [\n            "adcc946f-0095-4050-9236-0479d4ac6818",\n            "2974b78c-3d3d-4931-87e0-ac19e2d46609",\n            "4c48eaf5-fdda-45d9-bee3-3b8e4cd40cef",\n            "c29e53d9-bb6b-42e8-868c-71e718f7f73a"\n          ]\n        }\n      },\n      "draft": {\n        "data": {\n          "Date": {\n            "iv": "2020-09-25T05:00:00Z"\n          },\n          "title": {\n            "en": "Invasive Vine Spotted in Stearns County"\n          },\n          "description": {\n            "en": "<p>An invasive vine not seen in the United States in six decades has been discovered in Stearns County. "Important Property Tax Notice: Homestead Applications Due"\n        },\n        "description": {\n          "en": "<p>Property owners in Stearns County who have purchased or moved into a new home within the past year and need a homestead classification have until December 15, 2020 to file the application. The property tax homestead classification affects the amount of taxes that a property owner will pay in 2021 and may also affect the taxpayer&rsquo;s eligibility for a property tax refund.&nbsp;<\/p><p>A homestead application should be submitted to the County Assessor by December 15th if the use of the property owned or occupied as a qualifying relative has changed on or before December 1, 2020. Once homestead is granted, annual applications are not necessary unless they are requested by the County Assessor. Law requires notification to the County Assessor within 30 days of the change in homestead status due to a sale, move, or for any reason that would no longer qualify the property for the homestead classification.<\/p><p>A qualifying relative for homestead purposes depends on the type of property. For agricultural property, a qualifying relative includes a child, grandchild, sibling or parent of the owner or owner&rsquo;s spouse. For residential property it also includes the owner&rsquo;s uncle, aunt, nephew, or niece.&nbsp;<\/p><p><a href=\\"https://services.co.stearns.mn.us/homestead/\\">Apply for homestead classification<\/a>. If the property is located in the City of St. Cloud, go to the City&rsquo;s homestead web page at <a href=\\"http:///www.ci.stcloud.mn.us/619/Homestead-Applications\\">ci.stcloud.mn.us/619/Homestead-Applications<\/a>.&nbsp;<\/p><p>Contact <a href=\\"/450/Assessor\\">Stearns County Assessing Services<\/a> at 320.656.3680 or e-mail <a href=\\"mailto:property.assessment@co.stearns.mn.us\\" target=\\"null\\">property.assessment@co.stearns.mn.us<\/a> with questions. Sherry Kutter, a University of Minnesota Extension Master Naturalist, first spotted the vine along the <a href="/430/Lake-Wobegon-Trail">Lake Wobegon Trail<\/a> in Holdingford. Officials have identified it as rough potato (Metaplexis japonica), a type of vining milkweed.<\/p><p>Rough potato is native to eastern Asia. It has not been previously reported in North America except in 1958 in cornfields near the Iowa State University campus in Ames where it may have been part of a research project during World War II. How rough potato arrived in Holdingford is a mystery.<\/p><p>Bob Dunning, Stearns County Agricultural Inspector, mapped the vines locations and notified landowners. The densest infestations are along the South Two River near a ballfield. Bob said &ldquo;I was surprised by the number of locations I found it in once I began scouting for it. I&rsquo;m grateful to Sherry for discovering this issue before it had become even more widespread. Rough Potato is a very aggressive climber and it has an amazing ability to completely cover other vegetation.&rdquo;<\/p><p>Because of the magnitude of the infestations, the <a href="/238/Parks">Stearns County Parks Department<\/a>, Conservation Corps Minnesota (CCM), and the Minnesota Department of Agriculture (MDA) began removing thousands of seedpods, each containing many seeds. This was done to prevent the infestation from spreading. Based upon experience with related vining milkweeds, a combination of herbicide treatment and manual removal over several years will bring down the infestations.<\/p><p>&ldquo;While we may never know how rough potato got to Stearns County, we can be diligent so this and other invasive plants don&rsquo;t spread throughout Minnesota,&rdquo; said Monika Chandler, MDA Invasive Species Specialist. &ldquo;Seeds and plant parts like to hitch a ride, so cleaning equipment, pets, and our clothes before leaving an area can help prevent the spread of unwanted plants.&rdquo;<\/p><p>There are no vining milkweeds native to Minnesota. Both black and pale swallow-worts are vining milkweeds and have been found at a limited number of locations in the state. Property Tax Notice: Homestead Applications Due"},description:{en:'<p>Property owners in Stearns County who have purchased or moved into a new home within the past year and need a homestead classification have until December 15, 2020 to file the application. The property tax homestead classification affects the amount of taxes that a property owner will pay in 2021 and may also affect the taxpayer&rsquo;s eligibility for a property tax refund.&nbsp;<\/p><p>A homestead application should be submitted to the County Assessor by December 15th if the use of the property owned or occupied as a qualifying relative has changed on or before December 1, 2020. Once homestead is granted, annual applications are not necessary unless they are requested by the County Assessor. Law requires notification to the County Assessor within 30 days of the change in homestead status due to a sale, move, or for any reason that would no longer qualify the property for the homestead classification.<\/p><p>A qualifying relative for homestead purposes depends on the type of property. For agricultural property, a qualifying relative includes a child, grandchild, sibling or parent of the owner or owner&rsquo;s spouse.
